title: Zero defections: quality comes to services
harvard_reference: Reichheld, F.F. and Sasser, W.E., Jr. (1990) 'Zero defections: quality comes to services', Harvard Business Review, 68(5), pp. 105-111.
abstract_summary: Reichheld (Bain & Company) and Sasser (Harvard Business School) argue that service companies should treat lost customers as their equivalent of manufacturing scrap and manage towards 'zero defections', i.e. keeping every customer they can profitably serve. Drawing on Bain client case data rather than a formal study, they report that as companies cut customer defection rates 'amazing things happen to their financials': although 'the magnitude of the change varies by company and industry, the pattern holds: profits rise sharply'. The abstract gives three worked cases in which reducing the defection rate by 5% produced 85% more profit in one bank's branch system, 50% more in an insurance brokerage and 30% more in an auto-service chain, plus MBNA America, a credit-card issuer whose profits rose 125% after it halved a 10% defection rate. The mechanism is that long-standing customers generate rising profit over time (base profit, growth in purchases, lower servicing cost, referrals and price premiums), so defection destroys a stream of future value. The authors also present defection rates as a diagnostic: interviewing defectors shows where service falls short (Staples uses such feedback to find over-priced products), and retention targets should be reinforced through incentives (Great-West Life pays a 50% commission premium to brokers who hit retention targets; MBNA pays departmental bonuses).

claims_supported.claim: Reducing defections by 5 % can increase profits by 25-85 %; this is the origin of popular retention-economics multipliers, which are based on case examples rather than a general law.
claims_supported.where: Supported in substance, with two qualifications on wording. (i) The 5%-defection / large-profit-gain figure: the PubMed-indexed abstract states verbatim 'Reducing the defection rate just 5% generates 85% more profits in one bank's branch system, 50% more in an insurance brokerage, and 30% more in an auto-service chain', and 'when MBNA America ... cut its 10% defection rate in half, profits rose a whopping 125%'. The abstract therefore directly verifies a 30-85% range across three named cases. The commonly quoted '25% to 85%' range is the heading of the article's bar-chart exhibit covering nine service industries (the lowest bar, credit insurance, is 25%); that exhibit sits inside the paywalled full text and could not be opened in this session, so the 25% lower bound is verified here only via standard secondary attribution (Wikipedia, 'Loyalty business model': 'It is claimed by Reichheld and Sasser (1990) that a 5% improvement in customer retention can cause an increase in profitability between 25% and 85%', citing HBR Sept-Oct 1990, pp. 105-111). Either phrase the figure as 'between roughly 25% and 85% depending on industry' (standard attribution) or use the abstract-verifiable '30% to 85%' with the three named cases. (ii) 'Based on case examples rather than a general law': directly supported by the abstract's own hedging, 'Although the magnitude of the change varies by company and industry, the pattern holds', and by the fact that every figure is tied to a single named company or client case (one bank, an insurance brokerage, an auto-service chain, MBNA). The article is a practitioner piece built on Bain consulting case data, not a statistical study, so it is fair to say the multipliers are illustrative rather than a general law. (iii) 'This is the origin of popular retention-economics multipliers' is a statement about the article's influence on later practice, which the source does not and cannot make about itself; see the separate sub-claim entry below for how to word it.

claims_supported.claim: Sub-claim (attribution): Reichheld and Sasser (1990) is the origin of the popular retention-economics multipliers (the '5% retention = 25-85% profit' rule of thumb).
claims_supported.where: Not a claim the source makes: the article presents its case figures but says nothing about its own subsequent influence. The attribution is nevertheless well corroborated externally: OpenAlex records 5,279 citing works (W1594945480), Wikipedia's 'Loyalty business model' article attributes the 25-85% figure specifically to this paper, and it is the standard citation for the rule of thumb in the churn and CRM literature. Recommended wording: 'the widely repeated rule of thumb that a 5% improvement in retention raises profits by 25-85% originates in case examples reported by Reichheld and Sasser (1990)' - the citation then supports the figures and their case-based nature, while the 'widely repeated' / 'origin' framing is the report's own (defensible) observation, ideally backed by one secondary source that says so.

verification_notes: Crossref (query.bibliographic) did not return the HBR article itself - HBR did not assign DOIs to 1990 magazine articles - and instead returned only the German translation reprinted as a chapter ('Zero-Migration: Dienstleister im Sog der Qualitaetsrevolution') in Handbuch Kundenbindungsmanagement (Springer/Gabler, DOIs 10.1007/978-3-322-99638-1_6 [1998], 10.1007/978-3-322-99714-2_6 [1999], 10.1007/978-3-322-99464-6_6 [2003]); these are not the cited work and must not be used as its DOI. The doi field is therefore left empty: no DOI exists for the original article. Bibliographic details were verified from three independent sources that agree: (1) the publisher page hbr.org/1990/09/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services, which shows the title, authors 'Frederick F. Reichheld and W. Earl Sasser, Jr.' and 'From the Magazine (September-October 1990)'; (2) the PubMed record PMID 10107082 fetched via NCBI E-utilities XML: Harv Bus Rev, ISSN 0017-8012, 1990 Sep-Oct, Vol 68, Issue 5, pages 105-11 (i.e. 105-111), authors Reichheld FF and Sasser WE Jr, with the full abstract, which is quoted verbatim in claims_supported; (3) OpenAlex W1594945480: same title, authors, 'Harvard business review' 68(5): 105-11, PMID 10107082, DOI none, 5,279 citations. The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 (rate-limited) on every attempt, so OpenAlex was used as the fallback the task allows; the Semantic Scholar web page for the paper (3cf9e452adceb66ead134d9377ae8155016aa259) exists but rendered empty to the fetcher. The HBS faculty listing (hbs.edu item 9151) and HBSP product pages (90508-PDF-ENG, 519X-PDF-ENG) were blocked or empty (403 / bot-check). The Bain reprint page shows only an excerpt; its fetcher summary of 'almost 100%' should be ignored as it is not the article's own number. The full text behind the HBR paywall was not accessed, so the nine-industry exhibit (source of the 25% lower bound) is verified only via secondary attribution, as stated above. Two search hits offering the article as a downloadable PDF from unfamiliar mirror domains were deliberately not opened. Cite Them Right note: HBR is a magazine with volume/issue/pages, so it is referenced like a print journal article; if the student read it online, 'Available at: https://hbr.org/1990/09/zero-defections-quality-comes-to-services (Accessed: 27 September 2026).' may be appended. The suffix 'Jr.' appears in the publisher's and PubMed's author listing; 'Sasser, W.E.' without it is also commonly used and acceptable.
caveats: (1) Source type: HBR is a practitioner magazine, not a peer-reviewed journal, and the profit figures come from Bain & Company client cases rather than a designed study; present them as illustrative multipliers, not as an empirical law - which is exactly the framing the candidate claim adopts. (2) Meaning of '5%': in the article a 5% reduction in the defection rate refers to moving the annual defection rate by about five percentage points (cf. MBNA halving a 10% rate), not a 5% relative change; avoid re-expressing it in a way the source does not. (3) Range: the abstract verifies 30-85%; the 25-85% range is the article's exhibit heading known via secondary attribution, so quote it as 'between roughly 25% and 85%, depending on industry'. (4) Reichheld himself later warned that such cross-sectional profit-vs-tenure comparisons can mislead (Carroll and Reichheld, 1992, 'The fallacy of customer retention', Journal of Retail Banking, 13(4) - cited by Wikipedia; not verified in this session), which would strengthen a critical paragraph if independently checked. (5) The examples are banking, insurance, auto service and credit cards from around 1990, not telecoms; the Kaggle Telco dataset contains no profit or margin data, so the multipliers cannot be tested on it - use the source only to motivate why churn reduction matters economically.
